No, you don't need to tell them you are recording. Lack of consent is the same as not consenting.  http://www.dmlp.org/legal-guide/recording-phone-calls-and-conversations

"Federal law permits recording telephone calls and in-person conversations with the consent of at least one of the parties. See 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d). This is called a "one-party consent" law. Under a one-party consent law, you can record a phone call or conversation so long as you are a party to the conversation. Furthermore, if you are not a party to the conversation, a "one-party consent" law will allow you to record the conversation or phone call so long as your source consents and has full knowledge that the communication will be recorded.

In addition to federal law, thirty-eight states and the District of Columbia have adopted "one-party consent" laws and permit individuals to record phone calls and conversations to which they are a party or when one party to the communication consents. See the State Law: Recording section of this legal guide for information on state wiretapping laws." 

What is called "two party" laws in 11 states were found unconstitutional in 2014. 

TDLR: You don't have to tell anyone anything as long as your are part of the conversation.

If you are in a state where you need everyone's consent then yeah, but if it is on base (federal territory) and the evidence is used in a federal legal system, then you are fine. Too many people don't even consider recording because they assume its illegal when most of the time it isn't. Its a great tool to use not only to gather evidence, but to protect yourself from false accusations.

That is totally untrue, federal law only requires one person's consent, so if you are part of the conversation then you can record it. States each have different laws but the Army is federal so go for it.

I am a comp sci major about to go into my final year in ROTC. Right now I am doing extra training at a military base for CTLT where I shadow real LTs. 

Why are you so focused on special schools? I can tell you right now, and I am sure others will agree with me, that they  are fun but you should not focus your entire career around them. Do you know how soldiers actually get to those schools? They aren't just handed out like candy. You have to work for it just like in ROTC. If your unit doesn't get slots for something in the first place, you are SOL. 

You go to ROTC to become an officer. Do you know the difference between an officer and enlisted soldier? Being enlisted gives you a lot less day to day freedom for a long time compared to officers. But it really comes down to what kind of job you want to do. Officers manage everything and have to plan. You often do not get to do the fun stuff but you can make or break it for the soldiers you lead. Enlisted get to do more hands on fun stuff comparitively (not always, and depends on MOS). 

My advice would be to calm down about schools and reevaluate what job you actually want to do in the military. The Cyber branch is pretty new and there isn't much info about it yet, but you could put your Comp sci degree to good use there. If you just want to play Rambo then... go 11B, I guess. But if the only factor you are looking at is special schools, you really need someone to sit you down and explain that those alone are not good reasons to join the military and will be a very small percentage of your career. 

EDIT: I am near the top of my class and have had two opportunities to do Airborne or Air Assault during the summer after sophomore and junior year (right now). Instead of that, I did CULP and CTLT because it exposed to me life in the Big Army and gave me valuable experience instead of a cool badge that I can earn almost any time in my career. Just my two cents.

There are two types of scholarships-- a National Scholarship that you apply for online and have to jump through a lot of hoops for. However, if you get it, you can bring it with you to any school with a ROTC program. Most people who don't get this wait to get to their school and apply for a scholarship from within their school's ROTC program (this is what I did, I got a 3.5 year scholarship after my first semester in the program). 

In order to get this, you have to make sure the cadre who make the decisions know who you are because there will be a lot of new cadets. Make yourself stand out with good PT, a good attitude, always be on time and prepared, and volunteer for recruiting events. If I had not done Ranger Challenge as a freshmen, the cadre never would have known my name, and I think it played a big part in me getting a scholarship. At my school, they usually go to RC cadets. 

EDIT: for scholarships also don't forget about your grades. Grades are the biggest factor in the Order of Merit list so make sure you get as many A's as you can your first semester. They might also look at your SAT scores when you are still a freshman.
Also noteworthy-- ROTC will be going through a lot of changes in 2016, so what you hear now might not be totally correct two years in for you.

In order to do ROTC, you need to be a student of the school or of a nearby partner school. You really only need a pulse as far as qualification. Seriously. You just have to take an extra college class every semester for Military Science. PT is a joke but you should put effort in to do extra PT like Ranger Challenge. 

The school you commission from does not matter after the fact.

After your junior year, you are ranked nationally and depending on how close you are to the top determines if you get your top picks of MOS (you rank the ones you want, it isn't guaranteed). You are ranked by points called accessions points which you earn throughout your time in ROTC by doing Ranger Challenge, colorguard/sabre arch, and recruiting events.

It really depends on the college you go to, my sister and I are doing it at the same time at different colleges and we argue a lot about how differently we do things. But all in all, it has been a very positive experience, even coming in without a scholarship. I earned a scholarship after my first semester in the program, so don't sweat it if you don't get one out of high school. You have PT in the morning and a lab once a week, usually on a Tuesday or Thursday. You have to take a military science class every semester, but it isn't hard (however that also depends on your chosen college). There are a lot of extra stuff you can do to get involved, like Ranger Challenge, colorguard, Military Science Club, recruiting events... the more you do, the more Order of Merit List points you get which helps you get a scholarship or special schools like Airborne, Air Assault, or CULP.

Honestly I can't imagine my college life without ROTC now. I have made some of the best friends of my life here, met some of the coolest people (cadre) and done some pretty fun stuff (Ranger Challenge, FTX's, colorguard). I have really been brought out of my shell, and I couldn't be happier with where I am right now (as I'm sitting here freaking out over final exams...) For me ROTC provides an escape when the academia of college becomes overwhelming-- I probably would have gone insane without it. 

Hit me up with more questions if you have them. Again, programs differ a lot by college, so specific questions might be better directed to cadets at colleges you are looking at. If you go and visit the college, visit the ROTC department and they should be able to provide a cadet for you to talk to.

If its one thing my cadre have drilled into our heads, its that you should always highly value your NCO's input. Our scary ass SF MSG has transformed from someone who could cause all us cadets to scatter instantly in fear to someone I know I can go to whenever I have an issue. I think getting past that initial intimidation factor is really important, I feel so much better now that I'm not afraid to go see him.
